summary: This informational document gives an overview of the problems in deploying service functions, such as firewalls and load balancers, in large networks. Service function chaining describes defining and instantiating an ordered set of such functions and steering traffic through them.

plainLanguage.summary: Network traffic often needs to pass through several helpers, like a security guard then a counter. This note describes why setting that up is a hassle.

questions: why does topology matter for services
subtitle: Defining how to chain security and service functions in networks

tldr.problem: Networks deploy many independent service functions (firewalls, load balancers, etc.) that are tightly bound to physical topology, making them rigid, complex to manage, and unable to adapt to new services.
tldr.mechanism: Service function chaining separates these functions from topology using an overlay network, allowing traffic to be steered through an ordered sequence of service functions applied by policy rather than physical topology.
tldr.outcome: Enables operators to deploy flexible, composable services that work across virtual and physical infrastructure without topology changes.

facts.label: Service types mentioned
facts.value: Firewalls, load balancers, DPI, NAT, TCP optimizers, HTTP enrichment

today: RFC 7498 is an informational document that launched the Service Function Chaining working group. It remains the foundational problem statement; the architecture was defined in RFC 7665.

sections.title: The Problem with Today's Service Deployment
sections.content:
Networks deliver services by running service functions - firewalls, load balancers, NAT gateways, deep packet inspection (DPI) systems, and application acceleration boxes - that inspect or modify traffic. The problem is that these functions are tightly bound to the network's physical layout. A firewall must sit on the path that traffic takes, enforced by VLAN layout or routing rules. Adding a new firewall or reordering functions requires changing the network topology itself, which is risky and slow.

Current deployments treat services as locations on the network rather than as operations on traffic. This coupling limits where services can be placed, prevents rapid changes, and forces operators to manually configure each device's specialized rules. Services from different vendors rarely share information, so traffic may be re-classified at each function.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now, networks put service boxes in specific places and force traffic to go through them by rearranging cables. That is slow and hard to change. A new idea is to tag traffic and send it through services by rule instead of by where the cables go.

sections.title: Key Problems with Static Service Topologies
sections.content:
The RFC identifies twelve major problems. Topological dependencies mean that services cannot be relocated or scaled without redesigning the network. Configuration complexity arises because changing the order of services or adding a new function requires changing VLANs and routing everywhere, and operators fear the risk. Limited placement prevents operators from balancing load or using service resources efficiently.

Elastic scaling is hard because adding or removing capacity requires topology changes. Coarse traffic selection forces all traffic on a segment through all functions, even those not needed. Poor visibility makes troubleshooting difficult when services span data centers or administrators. Redundancy is constrained because backup services must sit in the same topology as primary ones.

The RFC also highlights problems with symmetric traffic flows (ensuring return traffic goes through the same functions) and multi-vendor interoperability, where services from different makers do not share classification results.
sections.plainLanguage: If you need to rearrange which guards check your bags, you have to move the physical booth. Firewalls copy traffic often, and nobody tells them what the others already checked. Backup systems must sit right next to the first one.

sections.title: Service Function Chaining Concepts
sections.content:
Service function chaining (SFC) is an architecture that decouples service functions from topology by introducing three key elements. A service overlay is a logical network built on top of the existing network using encapsulation or virtual links, carrying traffic through service functions without requiring topological changes to the underlying network. Services become resources that can be placed anywhere and accessed dynamically.

Classification determines which traffic flows into the service overlay and which chain they should follow. Classification can happen once at the network edge, and the decision is carried with the traffic, so each service does not need to re-examine it. SFC encapsulation carries metadata along with traffic, conveying chain information, the results of earlier classification, and policy decisions. This metadata allows services to make coordinated decisions without inspecting the payload.

These three elements work together: classification selects traffic, encapsulation tags it with the path and metadata, and the overlay ensures it reaches the right functions in order.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of making traffic go through physical locations, you mark it with a label that says 'go through guard A, then B, then C'. The label also carries information that each guard can add to. Services sit anywhere and read the label.

sections.title: Security and Trust in Service Chains
sections.content:
SFC introduces new security requirements. The service overlay is built using standard transport protocols like MPLS or VXLAN, and can add encryption like IPsec if operators require confidentiality and authenticity. Classification policy must be accurate and trusted, because it determines which chain a flow enters. Encrypted traffic limits classification granularity - operators can only use outer headers or external metadata to make decisions, not inspect the encrypted content.

The SFC encapsulation and metadata must originate from trusted sources. If needed, operators should authenticate the encapsulation and protect it during transmission. Multi-tenancy requires that tenant isolation be enforced by the network overlay, not by the services themselves, so that traffic from different tenants cannot be mixed.
sections.plainLanguage: Labels and metadata must come from trusted places. Encrypted traffic can only be sorted by outer tags, not what is inside. Different customers' traffic must be kept in separate chains.
